EQT unveils Middle East platform and Abu Dhabi office

Stockholm-headquartered EQT has become the latest GP to expand into the region with the launch of its Middle East platform and the opening of an Abu Dhabi office.

The office is the manager’s first on-the-ground location within its wider Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) platform, from which it aims to strengthen its relationship with regional investors, companies and partners, the firm noted.

The Abu Dhabi office will be led by the firm’s head of Middle East and senior executive officer, Smiyet Belrhiti. Meanwhile, EQT’s broader Middle East platform will be headed by Jimmy Mahtani, who will assume the role of chairman of GCC in addition to his current role as chairman of India and Southeast Asia for EQT Private Capital.

The Swedish firm is also expected to use the office as a strategic base to support its existing regional portfolio companies and to capitalise on the Gulf region’s increasingly important role in global capital flows, including its ambitious investment focus across digital and AI infrastructure.

The platform will be staffed by a dedicated local team, comprising infrastructure and private capital professionals, the firm noted.

Asia-Pacific real assets fund manager ESR – better known in private capital markets as a high-profile real estate investor – has agreed to acquire 100 percent of Aquila Clean Energy APAC, the regional renewable energy platform of German investor and developer Aquila Group.

The Aquila Clean Energy APAC portfolio comprises 1.6GW of operational, under-construction and “advanced development” assets across Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, Japan and Taiwan, across solar, wind and battery storage.

ESR began a push to diversify into infrastructure more than five years ago, with the launch of its first data centre fund, and has continued to explore opportunities in infrastructure that are at least adjacent to its core expertise in real estate.

The firm had been listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange since 2019 but was taken private in 2025 in a $7 billion deal led by a consortium of mainly real estate-focused investors, including Starwood Capital Group, SSW Partners, Sixth Street, Warburg Pincus, Qatar Investment Authority and OMERS.

This latest deal sees it expand its infrastructure capabilities yet further, with ESR president Phil Pearce saying the deal signals a new “phase of growth” for the firm, taking advantage of the “significant opportunities” at the intersection of logistics infrastructure, data centres and power.

The deal is expected to complete in Q1 2027, subject to customary approvals.

Data centre firms get yellow card for sustainability efforts

Just four data centre companies out of 50 analysed in a study by ratings and insights company S&P Global have disclosed net-zero targets.

Of the sample, 60 percent received a ‘yellow’ shade ranking, indicating that their actions are somewhat in conflict with a transition towards lower carbon emissions.

S&P assigned a ‘green’ shade to 26 percent of the companies, indicating they have detailed reporting and strategies around renewable energy procurement.

It does not expect any companies to achieve a ‘dark green’ shade – indicating a portfolio where a high proportion of assets use 100 percent green energy and minimal freshwater, among other factors – by 2030.

S&P’s report comes as scrutiny of data centres increases around the world.

US states including New York and Texas have imposed moratoriums on new data centre development, citing concerns about impacts on the environment, and on grid reliability, respectively.

Meanwhile in Australia, states are divided over the federal government’s dictum that all new data centres should bring their own renewable energy.

If you haven’t cast your vote yet to nominate who you think should appear in Infrastructure Investor‘s 2026 Rising Stars list, there’s still time to do so, but only until Wednesday, 30 September.

As always, we’ll be profiling the brightest young talents shaping the asset class. To be eligible for this year’s list, nominees must be under the age of 40 on 1 December 2026.

QIC expands its North America team

Brisbane-headquartered QIC is growing its New York-based team with the appointment of Yakov Tsveig as senior principal.

“This is a new role that expands our local expertise as we continue to build on QIC’s established presence in North American infrastructure over the past decade,” Marietta Moshiashvili, who since 2024 has been leading QIC Infrastructure’s North American origination and asset management activities, told The Pipeline.

“Having a local presence enables us to combine the strengths of a global platform with deep, on-the-ground experience, particularly in a market where we see compelling opportunities across power, renewables and the energy transition.”

In this new role, Tsveig will focus on origination, capital deployment and execution across power, renewables and energy transition investments, the firm said in a statement.

In addition, he will also provide support to QIC’s institutional clients, as well as supporting the management of QIC’s existing North American assets. These include Generate, CenTrio and Renewa, all of which are active in parts of the energy transition value chain.

He joins from Riverstone Holdings, where he most recently served as managing director, leading control buyouts, platform investments and financings across power, renewables, midstream and the energy transition.

From Infrastructure Investor Deals

CAI backs battery storage developer SMT Energy

Climate Adaptive Infrastructure, a California-based investment firm focused on sustainable infrastructure, has committed $268 million in common equity to US battery storage developer SMT Energy.

CAI had previously invested $32 million at project level in the form of structured equity, but its latest capital infusion marks SMT’s first outside investment at company level.

Founded in 2019 as an M&A platform focused on community solar in the US Northeast, SMT has evolved into an IPP, developing utility-scale projects, as well as powered land.

It has a portfolio of 14 operational projects – all located in Texas – with a total combined capacity of about 500MWh.

“Our plan is to scale to many multiples of what we’ve already constructed. We have the pipeline to support a company like CAI,” SMT Energy co-founder and co-CEO JJ Switzer told Infrastructure Investor Deals.

SMT’s largest project to date is Houston IV, with a capacity of 320MWh and a total cost of about $135 million, including about $25 million worth of equity. The project started operations in June.

The next phase of growth for SMT will be centred around the Southwest Power Pool grid, which runs all the way from the Canadian border to Texas.
